content.text: Radioactive materials can be extremely useful, but they also pose significant health risks. Understanding these hazards and how to minimise exposure is essential for anyone working with radiation. The principles of radiation protection apply from hospital workers to nuclear plant operators.

There is an important distinction between irradiation (being exposed to radiation from an external source, which stops when the source is removed) and contamination (having radioactive material on or inside you, which continues to irradiate until removed or decayed). Contamination is generally more dangerous because exposure cannot be easily stopped.
DNA damage can cause cell death
Exposure to radiation from external source
Stops when source is removed or shielded
Radioactive material on or inside the body
Continuous exposure until material removed or decays

| Feature | Irradiation | Contamination |
|---------|-------------|---------------|
| Source | External | On/in body |
| Duration | While exposed | Until removed/decayed |
| Spread | No | Possible |
| Protection | Shielding, distance | Containment, decontamination |
May appear years or decades later

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Dose | Higher dose = more damage |
| Duration | Longer exposure = more damage |
| Type of radiation | Alpha most damaging inside body |
| Tissue type | Some organs more sensitive |
| Age | Young people more vulnerable |
Alpha most dangerous (all energy deposited locally)

Alpha particles in contact with living tissue
All energy deposited in small area
A worker needs to handle a gamma source. Describe three precautions they should take.
Handle the source for as short a time as possible
Use long tongs to keep the source at arm's length
Store in a lead-lined container; work behind a lead screen
Additional: wear a film badge to monitor dose, never eat/drink in the area.
Compare irradiation and contamination as radiation hazards.

When discussing safety precautions, always link your answer to the three principles: time, distance, and shielding. For example, using tongs to handle a source increases distance, storing sources in lead-lined boxes provides shielding, and returning sources promptly reduces time of exposure.
— We receive natural background radiation constantly. Risk increases with dose.
— Lead is for gamma/X-rays. Different materials suit different radiations.
— You can wash off contamination, but not reverse the effects of irradiation.
— Irradiation doesn't usually make objects radioactive (neutron activation is an exception).
— Most radioactive materials look completely normal.

Students sometimes think that alpha radiation is the least dangerous because it is the least penetrating. However, if an alpha source is ingested or inhaled (contamination), it becomes the most dangerous type because its strong ionising ability causes severe damage to nearby cells and DNA.

Radiation causes harm through ionisation, damaging DNA and cells
Irradiation: external exposure; Contamination: source on/in body
ALARA: As Low As Reasonably Achievable
Monitoring: film badges, dosimeters, Geiger counters
Units: Bq (activity), Gy (absorbed dose), Sv (dose equivalent)
Risk depends on: dose, duration, radiation type, tissue, age

Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an external source; it stops when the source is removed or shielded, and cannot spread to others. Contamination is when radioactive material gets on or inside the body; it gives continuous exposure until the material is removed or decays, and can potentially spread.
— key distinction is source location and duration (comparison)

Externally, alpha is stopped by the dead outer layer of skin and cannot reach living cells. When inhaled, alpha particles are in direct contact with living lung tissue. Their strong ionising ability means all energy is deposited in a very small area, causing severe localised DNA damage.
— all energy deposited locally in sensitive tissue (reasoning)

Time: minimise the time spent near the source to reduce total dose. Distance: maximise the distance from the source, since intensity decreases with the square of distance. Shielding: place appropriate barriers between the source and people (paper for alpha, aluminium for beta, thick lead for gamma).
— three complementary strategies to reduce dose (recall + explanation)

The gamma source poses a greater external hazard. Gamma rays are highly penetrating and can pass through skin and tissue to damage internal organs. Beta particles are less penetrating and mostly stopped by the outer layers of skin or thin shielding, so they deposit less energy in deep tissue.
Staff stand behind a lead glass screen or leave the room during exposure. They also wear lead aprons to absorb scattered X-rays. These reduce the cumulative dose received over many procedures.
— shielding and distance reduce occupational dose (description)

Film badges contain photographic film that darkens when exposed to radiation. The degree of darkening indicates the total dose received over a period. This allows monitoring of cumulative exposure to ensure workers do not exceed safe dose limits.
— provides a permanent record of accumulated dose (reasoning)

Children have more rapidly dividing cells as they are still growing. Radiation is most damaging to cells that are actively dividing, because DNA damage during replication is more likely to cause mutations or cell death. This makes children more susceptible to both acute effects and long-term cancer risk.
— rapidly dividing cells are more radiation-sensitive (reasoning)
